newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK unemployment set for big November fall.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK unemployment set for big November fall.

text.p: UK unemployment data are set to show another dramatic fall in the jobless total in November but, despite the obvious labour market tightening, earnings growth in October is forecast to stay steady, economists said on Monday.
The Reuters consensus forecast suggests unemployment fell by 25,900 in November after October's massive 40,800 fall. This would reduce the unemployment level to just over two million.
The data are due on Wednesday.

"Last month's fall in the claimant count was distorted by the introduction of the Job Seekers' Allowance (JSA) and at least some of that will be unwound this month," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The government replaced unemployment benefit in October with the JSA which requires claimants to prove they are actively seeking work.
Last month, the Office for National Statistics said job centres were struggling with a backlog of claims which could have exaggerated the October jobless fall by up to 15,000.
"But over the next six months the JSA should reduce unemployment by around 35,000," Barr said.
David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders, said the series of sharp monthly falls is set to continue.
"It is clear the downward trend in unemployment has accelerated in line with economic activity and we expect this to be sustained for some time," he said.

Philpotts said other special factors are still at work pushing the unemployment tally lower. "It should be worth watching the estimates of how many claimants are falling off the register due to the fraud hotline."

The government introduced a telephone hotline in August for the public to report on benefit fraudsters. It has received over 100,000 calls since its launch and a spokesman for the hotline confirmed a large number of the calls concerned unemployment benefit.
Economists suggest the success of the hotline wiped around 6,000 off the claimant total in September and around the same number in October.

But despite the tighter labour market, economists said there is little evidence of increased upward pressure on earnings. The Reuters consensus forecast suggests average earnings grew 4.0 percent growth in the year to October, unchanged from September.

"Recent figures have shown a slight pick-up in wage deals to about 3.5 percent, reversing the small slowdown in (settlements) seen earlier this year," said Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers.
But he said this was still consistent with earnings growth of about 4.0 percent.
Most analysts believe lower unemployment and the growing number of vacancies will eventually push up wages, but perhaps not until next year.
"A tighter labour market will push both these (wage settlements) and wage drift higher, this is more of an issue for 1997," said Barr.
He forecast that average earnings could be growing by around 5.0 pecent by the end of next year.
